html:
Most of us know the feeling.

Whenever you play back a recording of yourself talking, the voice sounds strange, even off-putting, and you’d rather not keep listening.

You can’t help but ask your sis: why is that?

How did that sexy voice turn so creepy?

Is physics to blame, or is something else at work?

And behind it all,

is it twisted human nature, or total moral collapse?

Welcome to Ziyu Acoustics, the epic family-drama, tangled-emotions, popular-acoustics education show. Join Ziyu as we lift the veil on the mystery of the recording.

Two roads to the inner ear

The voice we normally hear when we speak reaches the inner ear, where the brain perceives it, by two routes: bone conduction and air conduction. One uses bone as the transmission medium, the other uses air. I explained in detail how we hear high and low pitches, and how the ear works, in an earlier answer:

How does the ear tell high notes from low ones?

Air conduction and bone conduction [https://www.alex-technology.com/]

Put a microphone in front of us to record, though, and the sound reaches the microphone through the air alone. That is exactly what happens when someone stands in front of us and listens to us talk. So the recording of your voice sounds the same as the voice other people hear when you speak. That’s why, when you play back a recording and cry out, “Do I really sound that awful?”, whoever is next to you will usually just shrug: “That’s how you always sound.”

Why do they sound different?

The question is: why should a different conduction path make the sound different?

First, when we hear ourselves speak, the high frequencies are attenuated whichever path the sound takes.

Air conduction: when we talk, our mouth faces forward, so the sound radiates mainly to the front. High frequencies do not diffract (bend around obstacles) very well, so less high-frequency content reaches our ears. Low frequencies diffract easily, so even though the mouth points forward, a large share of them bends back around to the ears.

Bone conduction: the skull conducts low frequencies more efficiently than high ones.

Sound traveling from the mouth to the ears [COMSOL]

Put together, this means the voice we hear while speaking is more muffled and deeper than the recording.

But that isn’t the whole difference. The key factor is timbre. Bone conduction and air conduction carry different speech sounds with different efficiency, and that efficiency also varies with frequency. So when the two paths add up, the gain changes from one frequency to another, and the timbre shifts. For the vowel /a/ (“ah”), for example, bone conduction is weak and air conduction dominates; for /i/ (“ee”), bone conduction gives the sound a strong boost around 2000 Hz [1].

The figure below shows loudness spectra for different vowels. When the sound we make reaches our own ears through bone and air conduction combined, its frequencies don’t change, but the heights of the formants (the peaks in the figure) do, and that changes the timbre. A microphone in front of the mouth, by contrast, records none of these changes, only a slight overall attenuation.

Loudness versus frequency for different vowels

[http://hyperphysics.phyastr.gsu.edu/hbase/Music/vowel.html]

Musical instruments help explain how changing formant peaks changes timbre. With our eyes closed, we can tell different instruments apart even when they play the same note. If “the same note” were nothing but a pure tone at a single frequency, they would indeed be hard to tell apart. In reality, every note brings a whole series of higher harmonics with it. Pluck a guitar string, for example. The note sounds its fundamental frequency (the animation at top left in the figure below), which describes one way the string vibrates. But besides this mode there are the other five in the figure, and higher-order modes beyond those. Each mode produces sound at its own frequency, and the frequencies are whole-number multiples of the fundamental.

Wikipedia

The video below shows why the same note sounds completely different on different instruments. Frequency runs up the vertical axis, time along the horizontal axis. Changes over time also make instruments sound very different, of course: the viola, for instance, varies strongly over time, which gives it a more “trembling” sound. Here we look only at the vertical, frequency axis.

In the video, every instrument plays the note at 128 Hz. You can see that the instruments reach different harmonic orders (the higher up the vertical axis, the higher the frequency and order of the harmonic). The cello, for example, has harmonics of very high order, which also shapes its timbre. Since there is not much energy at high frequencies, most of what we hear comes from the lower harmonics. And among those lower harmonics, the energy is distributed very differently from one instrument to the next (the darker the color, the higher the energy), with peaks in different places. So even if the changes over time and the harmonic orders were the same, these sounds would still differ in timbre, and so we would hear them differently. These harmonics correspond to the formants of speech. Because the formant peaks (energies) differ between hearing yourself speak and hearing your recording, the two sound different.

Different instruments playing the same note sound different

Video source: http://whatmusicreallyis.com/
The instruments, in order: piano, harpsichord, classical guitar, Indian sitar, viola, cello, baritone saxophone, bassoon, Japanese shakuhachi, accordion

One thing to note:

Everything above assumes lossless audio. There is a further reason: lossy recording. WeChat voice messages, for example, are heavily compressed, so they sound even more different. Think of them as an MP3 squeezed so hard that you can hear the drop in quality. If you’re curious, record the same passage with WeChat and with your phone’s built-in voice recorder, and hear how big the difference is.

Why don’t we like it?

It sounds different, so it feels strange. But why do most people find their recorded voice not just strange, but unpleasant, even unbearable?

Our voice does more than deliver the words we want to say. More importantly, it conveys a whole set of higher-level information: who I am, where I come from. How something is said is key to whether a message comes across precisely, and our voice carries the fine detail of that message.

And here’s the problem.

When we speak, most of our attention goes into working out what to say. When we listen to a recording of ourselves, we have time to analyze what we said, to notice how we said it, whether our pronunciation and intonation were appropriate, and so on, things we mostly miss while talking. And when we find that the impression we gave, the one we meant to leave, isn’t what we intended (which happens a lot), it stings.

This explanation has its limits, though. Most people rarely play back recordings of themselves talking. But politicians, singers, actors and the like watch their own videos and hear their own voices all the time, and with all that exposure they surely get used to it. Public figures also often train to express themselves well in public. So are they still embarrassed to hear their own voices?

Others dislike hearing their own accent on a recording. Take my fellow Northeasterners: we are convinced we speak as properly as a national news anchor, then we hear a recording thick with what people jokingly call the Northeast’s “corn-grits” twang, and we fall apart on the spot.

Then there are the kids born in the 2010s, after smartphones took over, whose parents have recorded countless gigabytes of video of them. They have long been used to their own image and voice. Will they ever know the pain of us old aunties and uncles?

What do you think? What makes you dislike, or like, hearing your own voice?

Main reference:

https://acousticengineering.wordpress.com/2018/12/21/why-do-we-dislike-hearing-a-recording-of-our-own-voice/

[1] Reinfeldt, S., Östli, P., Håkansson, B. and Stenfelt, S., 2010. Hearing one’s own voice during phoneme vocalization—Transmission by air and bone conduction. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 128(2), pp. 751–762.
